newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian toll rises, opposition urges U.S. help.
newsitem.headline: Algerian toll rises, opposition urges U.S. help.

text.p: Nearly two weeks of urban bombings and village massacres by suspected Islamist guerrillas have killed at least 170 people, Algerian newspapers said on Thursday.
Algeria's main secular opposition leader, Hocine Ait Ahmed, called on U.S. President Bill Clinton to appoint a mediator to help end the spiral of violence in the North African country.

He told journalists in Rome that Algeria was lurching toward total chaos and said France, which has close links with the military-backed government, had prime responsibility for international inaction.
Algerian state television reported on Thursday night that President Liamine Zeroual would address the nation at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Friday in a previously unannounced speech.

The television, which said it would broadcast the speech live, did not say what the address would be about but political sources said the president would most certainly try to calm a wave of fear gribbing Algeria after the upsurge of violence.

The sources expected Zeroual to reiterate his government's committment to the fight against the Moslem guerrillas and to dialogue with "legal" opposition parties on preparing parliamentary elections planned for the first half of 1997.
Analysts say the recent attacks are a message to Zeroual that Islamic fundamentalists remain a formidable force despite repeated claims the government has crushed them.

No one has claimed responsibility for the bombing campaign and other attacks, but the Armed Islamic Group (GIA) had threatened a 50-bomb campaign during the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan that began on January 10. In addition to bombs that exploded, at least 17 have been defused in the past three weeks.

In the latest reported killing of civilians by suspected guerrillas, El Watan newspaper said a boy and his father on their way to school in Saint-Maurice Douadoua village, 40 km (25 miles) south of Algiers, were killed on Wednesday.
More than 500 students and teachers have died since the GIA in 1994 warned students to stay away from schools because their studies hampered the guerrillas' "holy war".
Gunmen, thought to be Moslem guerrillas, ambushed a car in the same village the night before, killing two of the three people inside, said El Watan.
A bomb explosion in a market in the garrison town of Blida, 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers on Wednesday killed eight people and wounded 10, said the government-controlled newspaper El Moudjahid.

A car bomb also killed seven and wounded scores the same day at Quatre Chemins hamlet near Boufarik, 30 km (20 miles) south of Algiers, where 14 people were killed four days ago in another explosion, Algerian Liberte newspaper said.
"Algiers's residents have experienced a state of horror and they become scared by any suspect movement around them in the streets," said the Arab-language daily Al Khabar.

Ait Ahmed, leader of the Socialist Forces Front attending a conference in Rome, sought U.S. action. "One of the initiatives we expect is that President Clinton takes a measure likely to help bring about peace. Why doesn't he appoint a mediator on Algeria?"
But political sources told Reuters the Algerian government, which has rejected foreign involvement, would likely snub Ait Ahmed's proposal.
News reports say about 60,000 people have died in Algerian violence since early 1992 when authorities cancelled a general election that radical Islamists were set to win.
But Ait Ahmed put the toll at 100,000. "The current debate is either war or peace. The rest is secondary," he said.
